lessons.title: Business, industry & the course map
lessons.idea: Management begins with an activity that creates value. A business is an individual organization; an industry groups organizations with similar economic activities.
points: The introductory pages preserve the course outcomes, syllabus, assessment and assignment information.
Primary industries obtain natural resources; secondary industries transform them; tertiary industries provide services.
Quaternary activities emphasize knowledge and information. Use the examples and classification tree in the source to distinguish the categories.
Efficiency concerns the resources used; effectiveness concerns whether the intended result is achieved. Read the opening case with both questions in mind.
lessons.memory: A chain: obtain → transform → serve → know. This is a recall aid, not an additional classification.
lessons.question: How do business and industry differ?
lessons.answer: A business is an individual organization pursuing its activity; an industry is the larger group of businesses with related economic activities.

lessons.title: Levels, skills & five functions
lessons.idea: A manager coordinates people and resources. The five functions give the whole course its sequence.
points: Levels: top, middle and lower management. Technical, human and conceptual skills have different relative importance at different levels.
Top managers need a broad conceptual view; lower managers need more technical expertise. Human skills matter throughout.
Planning selects objectives and actions. Organizing establishes roles and relationships. Staffing fills positions.
Leading influences people to contribute. Controlling measures performance and corrects deviations.
lessons.memory: POSLC: Plan → Organize → Staff → Lead → Control. Imagine launching and running one organization.
lessons.question: Which skill matters most for a newly appointed CEO, and why?
lessons.answer: Conceptual skill: the CEO must understand the enterprise as a whole, connect its parts and set its direction. Human and technical skills still contribute.
lessons.trap: A function describes the work of managing; a Mintzberg role describes a pattern of managerial behavior.

lessons.title: The organization as an open system
lessons.idea: Departments affect one another. An organization takes inputs from its environment, transforms them and returns outputs.
points: Inputs include people, capital, information and resources.
Managerial functions coordinate the transformation process.
Outputs and feedback reconnect the organization with its environment.
Sub-systems must cooperate; optimizing one department alone can harm the whole.
lessons.memory: Input → transformation → output → feedback. Draw the environment around the whole loop.
lessons.question: Why is the systems approach useful?
lessons.answer: It shows the interdependence of organizational parts and the connection between inputs, transformation, outputs, feedback and the external environment.

lessons.title: Fayol’s 14 principles + 5S
lessons.idea: These principles help diagnose a management situation. Match each principle to a concrete clue in the case.
points: Work and authority: division of labor; authority and responsibility; unity of command; unity of direction.
Fair treatment and organization: equity; order; discipline; initiative; fair remuneration.
Continuity and coordination: stability of tenure; scalar chain; subordination of individual interest to general interest; esprit de corps; centralization and decentralization.
Unity of command means one boss for an employee. Unity of direction means one head and one plan for activities with a common objective.
The order discussion includes 5S: sort, set in order, shine, standardize and sustain. Check the source table for the Japanese terms and its additional safety column.
Centralization concerns where decision authority is concentrated. Its degree depends on the situation.
lessons.memory: Chunk the list into 4 + 5 + 5: work/authority, fair treatment, then continuity/coordination. Reconstruct each group before checking the source.
lessons.question: Explain unity of command versus unity of direction.
lessons.answer: Unity of command: one employee receives orders from one superior. Unity of direction: activities sharing one objective follow one plan under one head.
lessons.trap: Do not confuse equal treatment with identical treatment regardless of relevant circumstances. Equity emphasizes fairness.

lessons.title: Mintzberg’s ten managerial roles
lessons.idea: Ask whether the manager is working through people, handling information or making a decision.
points: Interpersonal: figurehead performs ceremonial duties; leader guides and motivates; liaison maintains contacts.
Informational: monitor collects information; disseminator shares it internally; spokesperson represents the organization externally.
Decisional: entrepreneur initiates change; disturbance handler handles unexpected problems; resource allocator assigns resources; negotiator bargains.
For a case, write both the role category and the specific role. The overview diagram is on page 55.
lessons.memory: People: F–L–L. Information: M–D–S. Decisions: E–D–R–N. Remember “collect, share inside, speak outside” for the information roles.
lessons.question: How do disseminator and spokesperson differ?
lessons.answer: Both communicate information. A disseminator sends it within the organization; a spokesperson communicates to outsiders.

lessons.title: Environment & corporate social responsibility
lessons.idea: Organizations interact with society. CSR goes beyond the firm’s economic and legal obligations.
points: Review the external-environment diagram on page 69; image content is retained in the source reader.
The classical view emphasizes economic performance; the socioeconomic view extends responsibility to society.

CSR drivers in the notes: employees and shareholders; brand equity; ethical marketing and social awareness; environmental consciousness; energy conservation and global warming; responsibility towards government.
Connect a CSR action to the stakeholder or social issue it addresses.
lessons.memory: People, brand, ethics, environment, energy, government: six reasons a firm feels responsible.
lessons.question: What distinguishes CSR from simply obeying the law?
lessons.answer: CSR includes intentions and responsibilities beyond legal and economic obligations, directed toward social welfare and stakeholder concerns.

lessons.title: Three ethical lenses
lessons.idea: The same decision can be examined through consequences, rights and fairness.
points: Utilitarian theory evaluates consequences: greatest good for the greatest number.
Rights theory protects basic rights such as conscience, speech and due process.
Justice theory emphasizes fairness, equity and impartiality.
Institutionalizing ethics means embedding ethical expectations in organizational practices. Read the source examples and measures, not just the three definitions.
lessons.memory: U–R–J: Useful consequences, Rights respected, Justice applied.
lessons.question: Which theory fits a decision based on impartial treatment?
lessons.answer: The theory of justice, because it asks decision makers to act with fairness, equity and impartiality.
lessons.trap: A favorable consequence alone does not establish that rights or fairness have been respected.

lessons.title: Trust makes change possible
lessons.idea: Change management helps people adapt when goals, processes or technologies change.
points: Change requires strategies for implementing and controlling the transition.
Trust includes integrity, loyalty, caring and keeping promises.
The notes extend trust beyond individual relationships to an organizational culture that lasts when leaders change.
lessons.memory: People change; a culture of trust should remain.
lessons.question: Why should trust extend beyond a single leader?
lessons.answer: Leaders may leave, while the organization continues. Trust embedded in organizational culture supports ongoing cooperation and change.

lessons.title: Culture & international management
lessons.idea: The notes compare management practices across cultural settings. Treat these as the course’s comparative descriptions.
points: Read the cultural dimensions and country examples in the source before using the comparison tables.
Japan: consensus, group harmony, long-term employment and extensive internal development feature in the notes.
USA: individual achievement, direct communication, faster individual decisions and performance emphasis feature in the comparison.
Korea: hierarchy, loyalty, seniority and respect for authority feature in the comparison.
The notes also discuss German, Austrian, Australian, Italian and British management. Compare the same basis across countries rather than writing disconnected lists.
lessons.memory: Compare using the same columns: decisions, employment, communication, relationships, leadership, motivation, conflict, development, change, work-life, evaluation, CSR.
lessons.question: Give three matched bases for comparing Japanese and American practices.
lessons.answer: Compare decision-making, employment practices and performance evaluation: the notes contrast consensus/long-term/group emphasis with more individual/performance/mobile employment emphasis.
lessons.trap: These are the PDF’s generalizations, not claims that every company or person in a country behaves identically.

lessons.title: Theory Z: a blended approach
lessons.idea: Ouchi’s Theory Z combines selected organizational practices rather than simply copying one country’s approach.
points: Long-term employment; consensual participative decisions; individual responsibility.
Slow evaluation and promotion; informal control with explicit formal measures.
Moderately specialized careers and holistic concern including family.
Use the Japanese-type and American-type organization lists to understand the comparison.
lessons.memory: Long employment, shared decisions, individual responsibility; slow promotion, blended controls, moderate careers, whole-person concern.
lessons.question: What is the responsibility pattern in Theory Z?
lessons.answer: Decision-making is consensual and participative, while responsibility is individual.
lessons.trap: Theory Z is separate from McGregor’s Theory X and Theory Y.

lessons.title: Planning & eight types of plans
lessons.idea: A plan connects a desired future result to action. Different types of plans answer different questions.
points: Purpose/mission/vision expresses the basic reason or direction; objectives state the ends; strategy gives the broad route.
Policy guides decisions; procedure gives a sequence; rule prescribes an action or prohibition without discretion.
Program combines activities and supporting arrangements; budget expresses expected results in numbers.
Planning asks what, why, where, when, who and how, and brings direction, coordination and a basis for control.
lessons.memory: Why exist? → What result? → Which route? → Decision guide → Steps → Must/must not → Coordinated activities → Numbers.
lessons.question: How do a policy, procedure and rule differ?
lessons.answer: Policy guides judgment; procedure specifies a sequence of actions; rule prescribes an action or non-action without discretion.
lessons.trap: A budget can express quantities such as labor hours, not only money.

lessons.title: Classify a plan on several dimensions
lessons.idea: One plan can have more than one label because each classification asks a different question.
points: Content: strategic, tactical and operational.
Time: long-term versus short-term; specificity: directional versus specific.
Frequency: single-use versus standing plans.
Strategic plans concern broad enterprise direction; operational or tactical plans translate direction into implementation as described in the notes.
lessons.memory: Content, time, precision, reuse: four questions to classify the same plan.
lessons.question: How does a standing plan differ from a single-use plan?
lessons.answer: A standing plan guides recurring activities; a single-use plan is prepared for a particular, nonrecurring situation.

lessons.title: The eight-step planning process
lessons.idea: Planning is a sequence from recognizing an opportunity to budgeting the selected course of action.
points: 1 Be aware of opportunities; 2 set objectives; 3 consider planning premises; 4 identify alternatives.
5 Compare alternatives against goals; 6 choose an alternative; 7 formulate supporting plans; 8 numberize the plans through budgets.
In an application answer, give each step an action in the same business case.
lessons.memory: Opportunity → Objective → Premises → Alternatives → Compare → Choose → Support → Budget.
lessons.question: What follows choosing an alternative?
lessons.answer: Formulate supporting plans, then express the plans numerically through budgets.

lessons.title: Objectives: hierarchy & multiplicity
lessons.idea: Objectives give planning a target. They can exist at different levels and may need to be balanced.
points: Enterprise objectives connect to departmental and individual objectives.
Top-down and bottom-up approaches relate objectives across the hierarchy.
Organizations usually pursue multiple objectives.
Quantitative objectives specify measurable amounts; qualitative objectives describe qualities or directions.
lessons.memory: Enterprise → department → person. Ask “what evidence would show achievement?”
lessons.question: Why is an objective hierarchy useful?
lessons.answer: It connects individual and departmental contributions to enterprise objectives and supports coordination.

lessons.title: Management by objectives
lessons.idea: MBO links agreed objectives with action, review and performance appraisal.
points: Superior and subordinate work with connected objectives and expected results.
Objectives should be clear and verifiable; review the source table of vague versus verifiable objectives.
The source process links inputs, agreement, actions and final review/appraisal.
Benefits include clarity, participation and commitment; weaknesses include poor guidance, difficulty setting objectives, short-term emphasis and inflexibility as discussed in the notes.
lessons.memory: Agree → act → review. The objective is the reference point throughout.
lessons.question: Why is a verifiable objective stronger than “improve performance”?
lessons.answer: It supplies an observable target against which achievement can be assessed; the vague phrase gives no clear basis for review.

lessons.title: Strategic planning & critical questions
lessons.idea: Before choosing a competitive move, understand the business, its environment and its direction.
points: Study the strategic-planning process diagram and corporate, business and functional levels.
Critical question analysis asks what the business is, where it is going, what environment it faces and what can achieve objectives.
Use the worked example to connect questions to a strategy instead of treating them as isolated definitions.
lessons.memory: Who are we? Where are we going? What surrounds us? What can we do?
lessons.question: Why does strategy need external analysis?
lessons.answer: External conditions influence opportunities, threats and the feasibility of achieving the organization’s objectives.

lessons.title: Blue Ocean & the four actions
lessons.idea: Blue Ocean strategy seeks new demand and value rather than relying only on existing competitive boundaries.
points: The notes emphasize value innovation and creating new market space.
Four actions: eliminate, reduce, raise and create. Apply them to competitive factors.
Advantages concern new demand and differentiated value; challenges include risk, resource investment and execution.
Work through the examples, competitive-factor analysis and four-actions diagrams in the source.
lessons.memory: ERRC: Eliminate the unnecessary, Reduce excess, Raise value, Create something missing.
lessons.question: Name the four actions in the framework.
lessons.answer: Eliminate, reduce, raise and create.

lessons.title: SWOT: sort the evidence
lessons.idea: The key is to classify by origin first and favorability second.
points: Internal + helpful = strength. Internal + harmful = weakness.
External + helpful = opportunity. External + harmful = threat.
Use the actual case statements. A competitor’s action is external; the firm’s own capability is internal.
Practice the exercise before checking the source classification.
lessons.memory: Inside = S/W. Outside = O/T. Then ask: helpful or harmful?
lessons.question: Is an emerging market opportunity or strength?
lessons.answer: Opportunity: it is a favorable condition outside the firm. A strength would be an internal capability to exploit it.

lessons.title: TOWS: turn diagnosis into action
lessons.idea: SWOT classifies facts; TOWS combines them into strategic responses.
points: SO: use strengths to exploit opportunities.
ST: use strengths to counter threats.
WO: address weaknesses by using opportunities.
WT: minimize weaknesses and threats; the notes connect this to defensive or retrenchment approaches.
Use the worked examples and the dynamic TOWS discussion to see that conditions can change.
lessons.memory: S can exploit O or resist T; W needs help from O or protection from T.
lessons.question: How is TOWS different from just listing SWOT?
lessons.answer: TOWS combines internal and external factors to formulate SO, ST, WO and WT strategies.

lessons.title: BCG portfolio matrix
lessons.idea: Two axes classify a business: relative market share and market growth.
points: High share + high growth = star; low share + high growth = question mark.
High share + low growth = cash cow; low share + low growth = dog.
Use the category to justify investment, cash generation or a selective/defensive response; read the source’s strategies and applications.
The product life cycle and portfolio steps provide context.
Limitations: two dimensions simplify a complex business, and interdependencies and other factors may be missed.
lessons.memory: Stars grow and lead. Cows lead in mature markets. Question marks grow without leadership. Dogs have neither.
lessons.question: How do a star and a cash cow differ?
lessons.answer: Both have high relative market share. A star operates in a high-growth market; a cash cow operates in a low-growth market.
lessons.trap: A shrinking market alone does not establish low relative market share. If a case omits an axis, state your assumption.

lessons.title: Growth & Porter’s generic strategies
lessons.idea: Competitive advantage and market scope are separate choices.
points: Read the growth-strategy slide before the generic-strategy framework.
Cost leadership pursues a low-cost position; differentiation offers something distinctive valued by buyers.
Focus concentrates on a narrower segment and may use cost or differentiation.
The notes warn about being stuck in the middle when a firm fails to achieve a coherent advantage.
lessons.memory: Two questions: cheaper or distinctive? Broad market or narrow segment?
lessons.question: What makes a strategy a focus strategy?
lessons.answer: Its restricted market scope: it concentrates on a specific segment rather than the entire market.
lessons.trap: An inexpensive product does not automatically prove broad cost leadership; inspect the target segment.

lessons.title: From plan to organizational structure
lessons.idea: Organizing establishes intentional roles so that people can contribute toward common objectives.
points: Identify activities; organize/group activities; classify or assign authority; build relationships between authority and responsibility.
Structure clarifies who does what and who reports to whom.
For a case answer, identify the step and attach the supporting action or quoted line.
lessons.memory: Activities → groups → authority → relationships.
lessons.question: What problem does organizing solve?
lessons.answer: It clarifies tasks, roles, authority and relationships so coordinated work can achieve organizational objectives.

lessons.title: Formal & informal organization
lessons.idea: A formal structure is deliberately designed. Informal relationships develop through people’s interactions.
points: Formal structure defines roles, reporting and authority.
Informal organization emerges through shared interests and relationships, illustrated by clubs and social groups.
The two coexist; an informal connection is not automatically an official reporting line.
Use the comparison table and overlaid organization diagrams.
lessons.memory: Formal = designed. Informal = develops.
lessons.question: Does an informal group replace the reporting hierarchy?
lessons.answer: No. It develops alongside the formal structure through personal and social relationships.

lessons.title: Tall, flat & span of control
lessons.idea: Span of control is the number of people one manager supervises effectively.
points: A narrow span tends to create more management levels; a wide span tends to create fewer levels.
Factors include subordinate training, delegation, planning, rate of change, communication techniques, activity, organization type and level.
Wide spans can reduce bureaucracy but overload managers; narrow spans allow closer contact but add cost and levels.
Read the source comparison for the full advantages, limitations and influencing factors.
lessons.memory: Wide → fewer layers. Narrow → more layers. Capacity decides what is workable.
lessons.question: Why can training permit a wider span?
lessons.answer: Trained subordinates need less continuous supervision, allowing the manager to supervise more people effectively.

lessons.title: Urwick’s ten organizing principles
lessons.idea: A useful organization aligns goals, keeps costs sensible and makes authority clear.
points: Unity of objectives; organizational efficiency; specialization; span of management; scalar chain.
Unity of command; delegation; parity of authority and responsibility; flexibility; functional definition.
Delegation gives people authority to achieve expected results; superiors retain responsibility for subordinate activities.
Functional definition makes expected results, activities and delegated authority explicit.
lessons.memory: Goals, efficiency, expertise, span, chain; one boss, delegation, parity, flexibility, definition.
lessons.question: Why must authority and responsibility be balanced?
lessons.answer: A person needs sufficient authority to fulfill assigned responsibility; responsibility should correspond to the authority delegated.
lessons.trap: Delegating work does not allow a superior to escape responsibility.

lessons.title: Departmentation: numbers, time & function
lessons.idea: Departmentation groups activities into manageable units. Choose the grouping that fits the work.
points: Numbers: group people by headcount; the source discusses conditions and limitations.
Time: organize by shifts to cover different working periods.
Function: group by specialized functions such as production, marketing and finance.
Functional grouping builds specialization but can create coordination difficulties between departments.
For an exam answer: name the grouping, draw a labeled structure, then give merits and limitations.
lessons.memory: How many? When? Which expertise? These identify numbers, time and function.
lessons.question: Which structure groups specialists by their work function?
lessons.answer: Functional departmentation.

lessons.title: Geography, process, customer & product
lessons.idea: The same organization can be grouped around locations, work stages, customers or outputs.
points: Territory/geography suits geographically dispersed operations and local needs; assess duplication and coordination.
Process/equipment groups around stages or specialized equipment.
Customer grouping supports different customer needs; product/service grouping focuses responsibility on outputs.
Read each source organization chart and its stated advantages and limitations.
lessons.memory: Where? How produced? For whom? Which output?
lessons.question: Which grouping fits a nationwide field sales network?
lessons.answer: Geographic/territorial departmentation is a defensible choice because work is distributed across regions and needs local coordination.
lessons.trap: A case may justify a combination of approaches. Explain which level uses which grouping.

lessons.title: Matrix structure & identification practice
lessons.idea: Matrix organization combines two dimensions, commonly function and project/product.
points: Specialists retain functional connections while contributing to projects.
The structure permits expertise to be shared across projects but requires coordination of authority.
Study the diagram before trying the final identification exercise.
Distinguish a matrix’s intersecting dimensions from a simple product hierarchy.
lessons.memory: Two dimensions cross: expertise × project.
lessons.question: Why can matrix structures create authority difficulties?
lessons.answer: People operate across functional and project relationships, which can create competing demands unless authority and coordination are clear.

lessons.title: HRM, HRD & their integration
lessons.idea: HRM manages people and employment arrangements; HRD develops people’s capabilities.
points: HRM includes policies, administration and managing human resources; HRD emphasizes employee development.
Use the source comparison for scope, objectives, functions and emphasis.
Integration supports holistic development, organizational performance and aligned people practices.
The notes distinguish managerial and operational HRM functions.
lessons.memory: Manage the employment system; develop the person. They support each other.
lessons.question: Give one reason to integrate HRM and HRD.
lessons.answer: People-management policies and development activities can reinforce each other, aligning employee growth with organizational needs.

lessons.title: Job analysis → description + specification
lessons.idea: Analyze the job before looking for the person.
points: Job analysis identifies duties, skills and knowledge required.
Job description describes the job: work, duties and responsibilities.
Job specification describes the person requirements: qualifications, knowledge, skills and other requirements.
When asked to draft both, use two clearly separate headings for the same position.
lessons.memory: Description = the job. Specification = the person.
lessons.question: Which document lists the qualifications a candidate needs?
lessons.answer: Job specification; the job description states the work and responsibilities.

lessons.title: Recruitment, selection & the ten-step process
lessons.idea: Recruitment attracts candidates; selection chooses among them; placement assigns the chosen person.
points: 1 Hiring needs; 2 job analysis/description; 3 sourcing; 4 screening/shortlisting; 5 interviews.
6 Assessments/tests; 7 background checks; 8 decision; 9 offer/negotiation; 10 onboarding.
Each step should follow logically: understand the role, attract candidates, assess suitability and bring the chosen person into the organization.
lessons.memory: Need → job → source → screen → interview → assess → check → decide → offer → onboard.
lessons.question: What is the main difference between recruitment and selection?
lessons.answer: Recruitment searches for and attracts prospective employees; selection evaluates and chooses suitable candidates.

lessons.title: Recruitment approaches, challenges & sources
lessons.idea: Source selection depends on the role and the organization’s talent needs.
points: Approaches in the notes include internal, external, campus, executive search, contingent, remote, diversity/inclusion, referral, social media, full-cycle and digital recruitment.
Internal sources listed: promotion, transfer, demotion, retired employees, notice boards and job posting.
External sources listed: press advertisements, educational institutes, placement/employment agencies, unsolicited applicants and employee recommendations.
Review the challenges slide, including talent shortage, competition, and time/resource constraints.
In a justification answer, explain how each source fits the stated vacancy.
lessons.memory: Internal = already connected to the workforce; external = attracting from outside. Follow the classifications in your source slide.
lessons.question: Why might promotion be useful for an urgent team-leader vacancy?
lessons.answer: The organization already knows the employee’s performance and experience, reducing familiarization needs and supporting internal progression.
lessons.trap: Employee recommendations are listed under external sources in this PDF; avoid silently changing its classification.

lessons.title: Selection: six stages & assessment methods
lessons.idea: Selection gathers different kinds of evidence about suitability.
points: Initial/preliminary interview → application form → reference checks → employment tests → interview → selection decision.
Read the test classifications and human-characteristic measures on pages 27–29.
The interview slide covers several formats; use the format’s purpose and features to distinguish them.
A decision should integrate evidence rather than rely on a single test or impression.
lessons.memory: Interview briefly → application → references → tests → interview deeply → decide.
lessons.question: List the six selection stages in source order.
lessons.answer: Preliminary interview, application form, reference checks, employment tests, interview and selection decision.
lessons.trap: The separate ten-step recruitment process places some activities differently. Use the sequence named by the question.

lessons.title: Training & development: process and trends
lessons.idea: Training supports capability. Its value depends on identifying a need and checking whether learning helps.
points: Needs assessment → design and development → delivery → evaluation → follow-up.
Six trends: digital learning, personalized programs, microlearning, gamification, DEI training and soft-skills development.
The source includes Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Starbucks and Walmart examples.
For “any three trends,” define each, connect it to a learning need and explain the expected benefit.
lessons.memory: Need → design → deliver → evaluate → follow up. Short learning units = microlearning.
lessons.question: Why is evaluation followed by follow-up?
lessons.answer: Evaluation checks the training’s results; follow-up supports transfer and continued improvement after delivery.

lessons.title: Training methods, induction & sensitivity
lessons.idea: Choose a method that fits how the skill should be learned.
points: On the job: apprenticeship programs, coaching, internship training and job rotation.
Off the job: conferences, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule training and programmed instruction.
Read the source’s induction and orientation definitions and comparison.
Sensitivity training develops awareness of interpersonal behavior and its effect on others.
lessons.memory: On = learning in work. Off = learning away from normal work. Use the source labels for induction/orientation.
lessons.question: Name two on-the-job and two off-the-job methods.
lessons.answer: On the job: coaching and job rotation. Off the job: case studies and vestibule training.

lessons.title: Systems approach to staffing
lessons.idea: Staffing links enterprise plans to available talent and future capability.
points: Enterprise plans → organization plans → number and kinds of managers required.
Compare requirements with the manager inventory to analyze present and future needs.
Use internal/external sources → recruitment, selection, placement, promotion or separation.
Appraisal, career strategy, training and development connect to leading and controlling.
The external environment surrounds the model; personnel policies and reward systems form part of the internal environment. Include feedback relationships.
lessons.memory: Plans → needs versus inventory → sources → staffing actions → develop/appraise → lead/control.
lessons.question: Why is manager inventory included in staffing?
lessons.answer: It shows existing managerial resources so the organization can compare supply with present and future requirements.
lessons.trap: The source diagram is image-based. Open page 46 to practice the full labeled sketch.

lessons.title: Developing excellent managers
lessons.idea: Manager development requires organizational support, useful information and continued learning.
points: Willingness to learn; accelerated management development; planning for innovation; effective measurement and rewards.
Tailored information; research and development in tools and techniques; managerial inventories; strong intellectual leadership.
Connect each consideration to how it improves managerial capability.
lessons.memory: Learn, accelerate, innovate, reward; inform, research, inventory, lead.
lessons.question: Why tailor information for developing managers?
lessons.answer: Managers need information suited to their roles and development needs to learn and make effective decisions.

lessons.title: Leadership: influence toward contribution
lessons.idea: Leadership influences people to contribute willingly and enthusiastically to group goals.
points: Read the distinction between managing and leading.
Review the ingredients of leadership and the qualities of an effective leader in the source diagrams.
Authority alone does not explain willingness; influence connects goals with people’s motives and situation.
lessons.memory: Lead = influence people toward shared goals.
lessons.question: What distinguishes leadership from merely issuing orders?
lessons.answer: Leadership seeks willing and enthusiastic contribution through influence, not only formal instruction.

lessons.title: Motivation & Maslow’s needs
lessons.idea: A motive energizes action; motivation is the drive to satisfy a need; a motivator is a technique; satisfaction is the resulting state.
points: Maslow: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualization.
Physiological: basic living needs. Safety: security. Social: belonging.
Esteem: respect and recognition. Self-actualization: realizing potential.
In a case, identify the unmet need using the employee’s specific statement. Multiple unmet needs may appear.
lessons.memory: Body → safety → belonging → respect → becoming.
lessons.question: An employee feels excluded despite adequate salary and safety. Which need is evident?
lessons.answer: Social/belonging needs are unmet. Connect the answer to exclusion and lack of group acceptance.
lessons.trap: Growth, recognition and belonging are different clues. If asked for the highest unmet level, inspect all the stated evidence.

lessons.title: Herzberg: remove dissatisfaction, then motivate
lessons.idea: Hygiene factors and motivators act differently. Removing dissatisfaction does not automatically create strong satisfaction.
points: Hygiene factors concern job context: policy, supervision, conditions, interpersonal relations, pay and security as shown in the source.
Motivators concern job content: achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself.
Analyze complaints about conditions separately from the absence of meaningful, satisfying work.
Read the Maslow–Herzberg comparison to understand overlapping needs without treating the theories as identical.
lessons.memory: Hygiene protects the floor. Motivators raise the ceiling.
lessons.question: Why can good salary coexist with low motivation?
lessons.answer: Salary can address a hygiene issue while achievement, recognition, responsibility or meaningful work remain missing.
lessons.trap: Do not say that removing every hygiene problem automatically produces motivation.

lessons.title: McGregor’s Theory X & Theory Y
lessons.idea: These are contrasting managerial assumptions about workers and work.
points: X assumes work is disliked, direction/control is needed and responsibility may be avoided.
Y assumes work can be natural, people can exercise self-direction and seek responsibility under suitable conditions.
Management practices should be linked to the assumptions and the situation.
Use the source comparison for motivation, control and responsibility.
lessons.memory: X = external control. Y = your own direction, with commitment and conditions.
lessons.question: Which assumptions support giving a capable team greater autonomy?
lessons.answer: Theory Y: people can exercise self-direction and accept responsibility when committed to objectives.
lessons.trap: These are managerial assumptions; do not permanently label every employee as an X or Y person.

lessons.title: Motivational techniques
lessons.idea: Techniques are practical ways of influencing effort, distinct from theories explaining motivation.
points: Compare positive and negative techniques in the notes.
Study the special motivational techniques, including money, participation and quality of working life.
For an application answer, connect the technique to the need or behavior it is intended to address.
lessons.memory: Theory explains why; technique describes what the manager does.
lessons.question: How does a motivation theory differ from a technique?
lessons.answer: A theory explains motivation; a technique is an action or method used to influence it.

lessons.title: Autocratic, democratic & free-rein styles
lessons.idea: The central question is where decision authority and freedom lie.
points: Autocratic: leader retains decision authority and directs activity.
Democratic/participative: members contribute to decisions.
Free-rein/delegative: employees have substantial freedom within the arrangement.
Learn each style’s strengths, limitations and suitable conditions from the source.
Style choice is influenced by the leader, subordinates and situation; justify the fit to the case.
lessons.memory: Leader decides → group participates → team has freedom.
lessons.question: Why might a creative, capable team benefit from participation?
lessons.answer: It allows members’ expertise and ideas to influence decisions and supports involvement; justify it using the team’s stated needs.
lessons.trap: No style is automatically best for every team and situation.

lessons.title: Likert’s four systems
lessons.idea: Likert’s systems form a progression in trust and participation.
points: 1 Exploitative-authoritative: low trust, centralized decisions and coercive direction.
2 Benevolent-authoritative: paternal confidence and rewards, while control stays largely at the top.
3 Consultative: managers seek input but retain important decisions.
4 Participative: substantial trust, group participation and shared involvement.
Identify systems from evidence about trust, motivation, communication and decisions.
lessons.memory: E–B–C–P: Exploit → Benevolent → Consult → Participate. Increasing trust is the spine.
lessons.question: What separates consultative from participative management?
lessons.answer: Consultative management seeks input while retaining major decisions; participative management involves groups more fully in decision-making.

lessons.title: The managerial grid
lessons.idea: Two concerns vary independently: people and production.
points: 1,1 impoverished: low concern for both.
1,9 country club: high people, low production.
9,1 task/authority-compliance: high production, low people.
5,5 middle-of-the-road: moderate concern for both; 9,9 team: high concern for both.
Practice placing each style on the axes and identifying it from cases.
lessons.memory: First coordinate = production. Second = people. 9,9 is high on both.
lessons.question: What does 1,9 represent?
lessons.answer: Country-club management: low concern for production and high concern for people.
lessons.trap: Read the axis labels before assigning coordinates.

lessons.title: Leadership as a continuum
lessons.idea: Leadership behavior can vary between manager-centered authority and greater subordinate freedom.
points: The continuum connects the manager’s use of authority with the area of freedom for subordinates.
Read the exact stages on the source diagram.
Explain a shift in style by saying how participation and decision freedom change.
lessons.memory: As subordinate freedom expands, unilateral manager control contracts.
lessons.question: What changes as we move along the leadership continuum?
lessons.answer: The balance between the manager’s authority and the subordinates’ freedom in decision-making.

lessons.title: Committees, groups & four development stages
lessons.idea: A committee has an assigned matter; groups involve interdependent people working toward common goals.
points: Forming: getting acquainted. Storming: conflict and clarification of objectives. Norming: agreed rules. Performing: task execution.
Read committee functions/formality, reasons for use and disadvantages.
Reasons include group judgment, representation and coordination; costs and delays are among the limitations.
Groups can influence behavior, attitudes, values, motivation and relationships.
lessons.memory: Meet → clash → agree → do. The notes use four stages.
lessons.question: What distinguishes norming from performing?
lessons.answer: Norming establishes agreed behavior and rules; performing focuses on carrying out the task.
lessons.trap: Do not add an extra development stage to a question asking for the four stages in these notes.

lessons.title: Teams & team building
lessons.idea: Teams need a meaningful purpose and coordinated contributions.
points: Read the team definition and the distinctions from groups and committees.
The source discusses recommendations, decision-making and operational roles.
Team building requires a worthwhile purpose, suitable skills, rules of behavior and commitment.
Study the team types in the final slide of this range.
lessons.memory: Purpose + people + rules + coordinated action.
lessons.question: Why do rules of group behavior matter in a team?
lessons.answer: They clarify how members work together and support coordinated effort toward the team’s purpose.

lessons.title: Communication: process & nine types
lessons.idea: Communication links people and integrates managerial functions.
points: Sender forms a thought and encodes a message; it is transmitted, received, decoded and understood; feedback closes the loop. Noise can interfere.
Formal and informal; downward and upward; horizontal/crosswise and diagonal; written, oral and non-verbal.
Each classification describes a different aspect: official status, direction or medium.
Compare advantages and limitations of written and oral communication using the source.
lessons.memory: Think → encode → transmit → receive → decode → understand → feedback; noise can interrupt.
lessons.question: How does diagonal communication differ from horizontal?
lessons.answer: Horizontal communication links similar levels; diagonal communication links different levels without a direct reporting relationship.

lessons.title: Communication barriers & remedies
lessons.idea: A message can be sent without being understood. Diagnose the obstacle and match a remedy.
points: Source barriers include lack of planning, unclear assumptions, semantic distortion, poor expression, loss/retention issues and poor listening.
Also review perception, attitudes, status/power, information overload and other barriers listed in the pages.
Remedies include clarity, audience awareness, consultation, suitable language and follow-up/feedback.
Read listening guidance and the separate written-communication checklist.
lessons.memory: Barrier → mechanism → remedy. Explain how the remedy fixes this barrier.
lessons.question: How can feedback help with unclear understanding?
lessons.answer: It reveals how the receiver interpreted the message so the sender can clarify or correct misunderstanding.

lessons.title: Controlling: the eight-step loop
lessons.idea: Control compares what happened with what was planned, then corrects deviations.
points: Standards → actual performance → measure actual performance → compare with standards.
Identify deviations → analyze causes → program corrective action → implement corrections.
Standards in the notes: physical, technical, monetary, managerial and time.
Use one consistent example across the entire diagram; distinguish a deviation from its cause.
lessons.memory: Set → perform → measure → compare → identify → analyze → plan correction → implement.
lessons.question: Why analyze causes before implementing corrections?
lessons.answer: The same observed deviation can have different causes; correction should address the actual cause rather than only the symptom.

lessons.title: Before, during & after: three controls
lessons.idea: The timing of a control helps identify it in a case.
points: Feedforward anticipates problems before they arise.
Concurrent control monitors ongoing transformation of inputs into outputs.
Feedback control uses results and reactions after the output.
Quote the time/action clue and explain why it fits the selected control.
lessons.memory: Before = feedforward. During = concurrent. After = feedback.
lessons.question: Monitoring a process while it runs is which type?
lessons.answer: Concurrent control: it gives immediate information about ongoing operations.

lessons.title: Exam-included self-study: budgetary control
lessons.idea: These source pages are explicitly marked as included for the end-semester exam.
points: Budgetary control compares actual results with budgeted results and supports corrective action.
A budget is a numerical plan; categories include financial, operating and non-monetary budgets.
Read the cash, capital and balance-sheet-related financial budgets and the operating budget categories.
Non-monetary budgets can state labor, space or output quantities.
Dangers include over-budgeting, overriding enterprise goals and inflexibility; read all source explanations.
lessons.memory: Budget = plan in numbers. Budgetary control = compare reality with those numbers.
lessons.question: Can a budget be non-financial?
lessons.answer: Yes. The notes include non-monetary budgets expressed in quantities such as labor or other resources.

lessons.title: Variable & zero-based budgets
lessons.idea: Different budgeting approaches handle changing activity and the justification of expenditure.
points: Variable/flexible budgets vary with output or another activity measure.
A fixed budget does not adjust in the same way.
Zero-based budgeting requires expenditure to be examined and justified rather than simply carrying forward the past.
Study the source’s explanations and cost behavior diagrams.
lessons.memory: Flexible asks “what if volume changes?” Zero-based asks “why spend this at all?”
lessons.question: Why is a variable budget useful when output changes?
lessons.answer: It adjusts budgeted amounts to the activity level, making comparison more meaningful.

lessons.title: Non-budgetary controls & project networks
lessons.idea: Not all useful control information is a budget.
points: Statistical data; special reports and analysis; operational audit; other devices listed on the source overview.
Operational audit independently appraises operations and their effectiveness.
PERT and CPM support project planning and control; Gantt charts show time relationships.
Review the time-event network material and source diagrams rather than substituting a financial budget.
lessons.memory: Data tells, reports explain, audit appraises, networks schedule.
lessons.question: How does a Gantt chart support control?
lessons.answer: It shows activities or events against time, helping managers compare progress with the schedule.

lessons.title: Overall control: summaries, profit & ROI
lessons.idea: Overall control assesses the enterprise or a major unit rather than only isolated operations.
points: Budget summaries consolidate individual budgets and show overall performance.
Profit-and-loss control compares revenue and expenses and gives divisional managers responsibility for results.
Read its limitations, including accounting effort and overhead allocation issues.
ROI relates profit to investment; the source diagram links return to its influencing factors.
Study ROI advantages and limitations, including the information and valuation difficulties in the notes.
lessons.memory: Whole-enterprise lens: combined budgets → profit/loss → return on invested resources.
lessons.question: What does ROI add beyond simply knowing profit?
lessons.answer: It relates profit to the investment used to produce it, supporting comparison of how effectively invested resources are used.

lessons.title: Direct & preventive control
lessons.idea: Direct control investigates deviations; preventive control improves managers so fewer avoidable deviations arise.
points: Direct control traces causes and responsibility for unsatisfactory results.
Read the seven causes/assumptions discussion on negative deviations.
Preventive control develops knowledge and application of managerial principles, functions and techniques.
Study the three assumptions and the advantages: psychological benefit, accuracy, self-control and lighter managerial burden.
lessons.memory: Direct: trace the error. Preventive: improve the capability that avoids it.
lessons.question: How is preventive control connected to manager development?
lessons.answer: Improved managerial knowledge and capability reduce errors that would otherwise require corrective action.
lessons.trap: Do not collapse this managerial concept into merely another label for feedforward control.

lessons.title: Quality starts with the customer
lessons.idea: Quality concerns meeting requirements and needs, not simply making something expensive or durable.
points: Juran emphasizes features that meet customer needs and freedom from deficiencies.
Products include goods, software and services; customers may be external or internal.
Concepts include fitness for purpose, conformance to requirements and grade.
Quality of design translates customer needs into the product’s intended features and specifications.
lessons.memory: Need → specification. A durable fuse that fails to protect is not good quality for its purpose.
lessons.question: Why is durability alone an inadequate definition of quality?
lessons.answer: A product must serve its intended purpose and requirements; the source’s fuse example shows that lasting longer can be undesirable.

lessons.title: Design, conformance & performance
lessons.idea: A good idea, correct manufacture and satisfactory use are different links in the quality chain.
points: Design: specify the right product for the need.
Conformance: the actual output follows the design and other requirements; process variability and inspection matter.
Performance: how the product functions in customer use, depending on both design and conformance.
Review the listed factors affecting conformance and the service-sector example.
lessons.memory: Design = intended. Conformance = made as intended. Performance = works in use.
lessons.question: Can perfect conformance compensate for a poor design?
lessons.answer: No. A product can match its design precisely yet fail to satisfy the customer if the design itself is unsuitable.

lessons.title: Quality control & specifications
lessons.idea: QC measures actual performance, compares it with a standard and acts on deviation.
points: Quality belongs across marketing, R&D, design, planning, purchasing, production, inspection and retail/service.
Specifications can be standard, customer or company specifications.
QC seeks acceptable output, fewer defects and losses, conformity, loyal customers and sustained value.
Key characteristics include technological, psychological, time-oriented, contractual and ethical dimensions.
Inspection finds defects; QC aims to regulate quality and reduce variation in future output.
lessons.memory: Measure → compare → correct. Inspection detects; QC feeds improvement.
lessons.question: Give three objectives of quality control.
lessons.answer: Improve customer acceptance, reduce losses from defects and ensure conformity to established standards; connect them to customer satisfaction.

lessons.title: Stakeholders in quality
lessons.idea: People affected by an organization can influence its quality decisions and their success.
points: Stakeholders include investors, consumers, employees and other affected or influential groups.
Roles include plan/policy development, support for improvement initiatives and performance monitoring.
Quality assurance begins by considering confidence in product performance under actual conditions.
lessons.memory: Help plan → support improvement → monitor progress.
lessons.question: Why involve stakeholders early in a quality initiative?
lessons.answer: Their interests and support affect implementation; involvement helps identify concerns and align the initiative with relevant needs.

lessons.title: Quality assurance, audit & survey
lessons.idea: Assurance builds confidence that quality requirements will be met. Audits and surveys examine whether arrangements support that confidence.
points: Read the detailed quality-assurance explanation before the audit process.
Quality audit examines quality activities and their effectiveness systematically.
The notes discuss audit planning, evidence, reporting and follow-up; preserve the full procedure in the source.
Quality survey evaluates a supplier’s quality capabilities and arrangements.
lessons.memory: Assurance = confidence supported by evidence. Audit = examine. Survey = assess capability.
lessons.question: How is assurance broader than inspecting the finished product?
lessons.answer: It concerns confidence in the arrangements and activities that support quality, not just sorting finished output.

lessons.title: Product audits & economic effects
lessons.idea: Product audits independently evaluate quality and help reveal defects missed earlier.
points: Read the defect classifications, demerit weighting and example table.
Inspection effectiveness example: 40 previously detected defects out of 50 total detected defects = 80%.
Compare against a stable base period or market quality as described.
Quality affects costs through fewer deficiencies and income through valued product features.
lessons.memory: Fewer deficiencies → lower waste. Better features → greater customer value.
lessons.question: In the source example, what is inspection effectiveness if inspection found 40 defects and audit found 10 more?
lessons.trap: Do not divide by only the additional audit defects.

lessons.title: Quality foundations: summary & worked answers
lessons.idea: Use the unit’s own summary, keywords and SAQ answers to test whether the distinctions have become clear.
points: Review quality, QC, assurance, audit and the effects on cost and income.
Work through the supplied self-assessment answers.
Explain the complete chain from customer need through product design, conformance, use and feedback.
lessons.memory: Need → design → make → check → use → learn.
lessons.question: How can quality simultaneously reduce costs and increase income?
lessons.answer: Freedom from deficiencies reduces waste, rework and user losses; useful features improve satisfaction, sales and market position.

lessons.title: TQM, objectives & Joiner’s triangle
lessons.idea: TQM makes quality a shared, continuing organizational commitment.
points: Study the definition, principle of objectives and reasons for popularity.
Three axioms: commitment, scientific knowledge and involvement; represented by Joiner’s triangle.
Management commitment requires action and resources, not slogans alone.
Scientific methods support fact-based decisions; involvement brings people, teams and suppliers into improvement.
Benefits discussed include cost reduction, a supportive environment and broader measures of success.
lessons.memory: CSI: Commitment + Scientific knowledge + Involvement. All three sides must support the culture.
lessons.question: State and explain the three TQM axioms.
lessons.answer: Commitment sustains improvement; scientific knowledge supplies appropriate tools and evidence; involvement engages everyone in the change.

lessons.title: The seven basic tools in your PDF
lessons.idea: Choose a tool by the question you need to answer.
points: Cause-and-effect/fishbone: possible causes. Flowchart: process steps. Pareto: priorities among causes.
Run chart: change over time. Control chart: process behavior with control limits.
Correlation chart: relationship between factors. Histogram: frequency distribution.
The source illustrates mean, standard deviation and UCL/LCL calculations and a histogram example.
Keep this exact seven-tool list: other textbooks may use a different list.
lessons.memory: Causes, steps, priorities, time, limits, relationships, distribution.
lessons.question: Which tool helps prioritize the largest causes of defects?
lessons.answer: A Pareto chart, which arranges causes by magnitude so the most significant contributors can be addressed first.
lessons.trap: The PDF’s list includes flowchart and run chart. Do not substitute an external “standard seven” list.

lessons.title: Kaizen, Kanban, circles & maintenance
lessons.idea: Small continuing improvements need people, flow and reliable equipment.
points: Read the Kaizen introduction at the end of page 9 with the tools lesson.
Total quality control integrates quality across organizational groups.
Kanban supports just-in-time flow; quality circles bring small groups into improvement.
The source calls TPM “Total Predictive Maintenance”; use its discussion and terminology for this course.
lessons.memory: Improve continually; pull materials; discuss locally; maintain equipment.
lessons.question: How do quality circles support improvement?
lessons.answer: Small groups use participation and shared experience to identify and solve quality-related problems.
lessons.trap: Retain the terminology used in the supplied PDF; do not silently replace its TPM expansion.

lessons.title: Deming’s 14 points, seven sins & PDCA
lessons.idea: Deming connects quality to improving the system and management’s behavior.
points: 14 points, grouped for recall: constancy and new philosophy; prevention rather than mass inspection; avoid price-only purchasing; continually improve.
Train, lead, remove fear and break barriers; eliminate slogans and numerical targets/work standards.
The PDF’s list continues with ending annual merit reviews, education/self-improvement and permanent top-management commitment.
Read all seven deadly sins on pages 14–15; they include lack of constancy, short-term emphasis and management practices that undermine improvement.
PDCA: plan, do, check, act. Use the cycle as a repeating learning loop.
lessons.memory: Direction → better system → better leadership → remove obstacles → learn and commit. PDCA: plan a change, try it, check it, act on learning.
lessons.question: What is the order of the PDCA cycle?
lessons.answer: Plan → Do → Check → Act; repeat the cycle for continued improvement.
lessons.trap: Use the 14-point wording in this PDF; do not merge it with Crosby’s different 14 points.

lessons.title: Juran’s trilogy & breakthrough
lessons.idea: Juran separates setting up quality, maintaining it and raising it to a better level.
points: Quality planning identifies customers/needs, translates them into requirements and develops product/process capability.
Quality control detects and corrects adverse change.
Quality improvement raises performance beyond the previous level.
Read the breakthrough sequence, managerial responsibilities and project-by-project approach.
lessons.memory: Plan the level → control the level → improve the level.
lessons.question: Why is improvement different from control?
lessons.answer: Control prevents or corrects deterioration from the set level; improvement establishes a higher level of quality.

lessons.title: Crosby: four absolutes & zero defects
lessons.idea: Crosby makes requirements and the cost of doing things wrong central to quality management.
points: Quality means conformance to requirements; the system is prevention; the measurement is price of non-conformance; the performance standard is zero defects.
Zero defects is a continuing improvement objective; the notes warn that slogans without a sound system or unrealistic short-term pressure can fail.
Read Crosby’s separate 14-point improvement program on pages 21–22.
Review the steps for implementing a zero-defect program on page 23.
lessons.memory: Conformance → prevention → zero defects → cost of non-conformance. Use these four labels to reconstruct the explanation.
lessons.question: What is the price of non-conformance?
lessons.answer: The costs of doing things wrong, such as rejects, rework and warranty costs.
lessons.trap: “Quality is free” does not mean improvement requires no effort; it concerns the savings from avoiding poor quality.

lessons.title: Poka-yoke & concurrent engineering
lessons.idea: Quality improves when errors are prevented and product decisions are coordinated early.
points: Poka-yoke concerns mistake-proofing: preventing mistakes or making them evident.
Concurrent engineering coordinates product and related process considerations rather than leaving everything to a late sequence.
Read the unit summary and keywords, then answer its SAQs without looking.
lessons.memory: Poka-yoke: stop the mistake. Concurrent: work together early.
lessons.question: How does poka-yoke support quality?
lessons.answer: It helps prevent errors or detect them promptly, reducing the chance that mistakes become defects.

lessons.title: The house of TQM: eight elements
lessons.idea: The PDF gives a ready-made memory picture: quality culture as a house.
points: Foundation: ethics, integrity, trust.
Bricks: training, teamwork, leadership.
Mortar: communication. Roof: recognition.
Read the team types, communication directions and recognition discussion within these pages.
The components depend on each other; recognition cannot compensate for an untrustworthy foundation.
lessons.memory: Foundation EIT; bricks TTL; communication binds; recognition crowns.
lessons.question: List the eight elements of TQM.
lessons.answer: Ethics, integrity, trust, training, teamwork, leadership, communication and recognition.

lessons.title: Affinity, tree & interrelations diagrams
lessons.idea: Different diagrams make different relationships visible.
points: Affinity groups related ideas or verbal information.
Tree breaks a broad objective into more specific means/actions.
Interrelations shows cause-and-effect links among issues and identifies drivers/effects.
Follow the source construction steps and arrow-counting example.
lessons.memory: Affinity groups. Tree decomposes. Interrelations connects causes.
lessons.question: Which tool decomposes a broad objective into specific actions?
lessons.answer: A tree diagram.

lessons.title: Prioritization & PDPC
lessons.idea: One tool chooses where to act; the other prepares for what could go wrong.
points: Prioritization matrices evaluate options against criteria and ratings; the introductory explanation begins on page 9.
PDPC maps a proposed process or plan, possible outcomes and countermeasures.
Study the scoring tables and the lawnmower-related example.
When explaining a tool, state its purpose, construction and interpretation.
lessons.memory: Prioritization = choose. PDPC = anticipate problems and responses.
lessons.question: What is PDPC used for?
lessons.answer: To anticipate possible problems or outcomes in a planned process and prepare appropriate countermeasures.

lessons.title: Activity networks & matrix diagrams
lessons.idea: Networks organize tasks through time; matrices organize relationships between sets of factors.
points: Activity network/PERT shows dependencies, parallel activities and scheduling.
Review activities, events, paths, dummy activities and construction rules in the source.
The expected-time example uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates; inspect the worked figure and SAQ.
Matrix diagrams show presence and strength of relationships; review the restaurant example and matrix types.
lessons.memory: Network = sequence through time. Matrix = intersections between factor sets.
lessons.question: What does a matrix diagram reveal?
lessons.answer: Whether relationships exist between sets of factors and how strong those relationships are.
lessons.trap: A matrix diagram here is a quality tool, not the matrix organization structure in Module 3.

lessons.title: Implementing TQM
lessons.idea: Implementation depends on the organization’s condition and its capacity for change.
points: The notes discuss different organizational scenarios and readiness.
Compare integrated-management and traditional-management approaches.
Guidelines include commitment, a shared direction, customer identification/feedback, quality teams and organizational assessment.
Read the full sequence rather than assuming a single universal implementation formula.
lessons.memory: Assess readiness → align people → act on quality → learn from results.
lessons.question: Why should organizational readiness be assessed before implementing TQM?
lessons.answer: Its history, culture and ability to change affect the approach and support required for successful implementation.

lessons.title: Measure quality: cost, time & scorecards
lessons.idea: Measurement gives feedback about whether improvement is working.
points: Cost of poor quality is introduced on page 17 and continued here: waste and non-value-adding activity consume resources.
Improper time management leaves more effort in firefighting and less in prevention.
Scorekeeping makes results visible and enables comparison with objectives.
Read the cost figures, time-management comparison, scorecard and final keywords.
lessons.memory: Cost shows waste. Time shows where effort goes. Scorecards show progress.
lessons.question: Why distinguish firefighting time from prevention time?
lessons.answer: It reveals whether effort is consumed by recurring problems or invested in preventing them.

lessons.title: ISO 9000: purpose, family & benefits
lessons.idea: These pages describe quality-management-system standards and their historical development.
points: ISO 9000 concerns management systems and quality assurance practices, rather than certifying that every individual product is perfect.
Read the history and the source’s original ISO 9000/9001/9002/9003/9004/8402 descriptions.
The PDF then explains the revised ISO 9000:2000 family: vocabulary, requirements and improvement guidance.
Benefits include confidence, consistency, market access and improved organization, as elaborated in the pages.
lessons.memory: A system for consistent quality. Learn the version labels along with the roles.
lessons.question: Does ISO 9000 simply specify the quality of a single product?
lessons.answer: No. The supplied unit focuses on the organization’s quality management and assurance system.
lessons.trap: Historical syllabus content: these notes discuss 1994/2000 versions. This app preserves them for your exam and does not present them as current regulatory guidance.

lessons.title: QMS requirements & management responsibility
lessons.idea: A quality system connects policy, resources, product realization, measurement and improvement.
points: Read the requirements in the source: management commitment, customer focus, policy, planning, responsibilities and review.
Resource management supports competent people and appropriate infrastructure/work environment.
Product realization covers planning, customer processes, design, purchasing and production/service control.
Measurement, analysis and improvement include monitoring, non-conforming output and corrective/preventive action.
lessons.memory: Direction → resources → realization → measurement → improvement.
lessons.question: What should happen when a non-conforming product is detected?
lessons.answer: Identify and control it to prevent unintended use/delivery, address the cause and retain evidence of correction as described in the PDF.

lessons.title: Documentation: say, do, show
lessons.idea: Documentation communicates methods, supports consistent action and provides evidence.
points: Read page 9 with the preceding lesson for the quality manual and six required documented procedures in the source edition.
Those six: document control, record control, internal audit, non-conforming product control, corrective action and preventive action.
Other documents include specifications, quality plans and records.
A document provides information; a record provides evidence of results or activities.
lessons.memory: Manual = system. Procedure = method. Record = evidence.
lessons.question: How does a record differ from a procedure?
lessons.answer: A procedure specifies how an activity is performed; a record provides evidence of results achieved or activities performed.

lessons.title: Implementing ISO 9000 QMS
lessons.idea: Implementation moves from understanding and documentation to internal correction and external assessment.
points: Exposure/training → draft quality manual → internal audit and incorporation of requirements → external certification audit.
The notes distinguish organizations starting a QMS, adapting an existing QMS and demonstrating conformity.
Documentation also supports communication, evidence and knowledge sharing.
Read the differences between existing process-based arrangements and arrangements needing more definition.
lessons.memory: Train → document → audit inside → correct → assess outside.
lessons.question: Why conduct an internal audit before external assessment?
lessons.answer: It checks existing practices against requirements and allows deficiencies to be corrected before external evaluation.

lessons.title: Occupational safety & OSHA
lessons.idea: The unit connects quality management with safe and healthy work.
points: Read OSHA’s purposes and the benefits to employers, employees and the public as described in the course material.
Standard categories: specification, performance, particular/vertical and general/horizontal.
Safety assessment uses documentation, interviews and site-condition review.
Key components include leadership/participation/accountability, worksite analysis, hazard prevention/control and safety/health training.
The source explains why awareness campaigns alone may not ensure safe practice.
lessons.memory: Lead and involve → analyze the site → prevent/control hazards → train.
lessons.question: Name three ways to assess a safety program in the source.
lessons.answer: Review documents, interview people and inspect site conditions.
lessons.trap: Study this as supplied course content, not as advice on current legal compliance.

lessons.title: ISO 14000 & final quality review
lessons.idea: Environmental management connects the organization’s activities and product life cycle to environmental effects.
points: Read the ISO 14000 explanation beginning on page 17 with the preceding lesson.
The source covers environmental policy, auditing, performance evaluation, labeling and life-cycle assessment.
Policy requires senior-management support and commitments to improvement, pollution prevention and applicable requirements.
The cycle involves planning, implementation/operation, checking/corrective action and management review.
Review the summary, glossary and SAQs. The bibliography is retained as source material, not added to the syllabus.
lessons.memory: 9000: quality system. 14000: environmental system. OSHA: worker safety and health.
lessons.question: How do ISO 9000 and ISO 14000 differ in focus?
lessons.answer: ISO 9000 focuses on quality management/customer satisfaction; ISO 14000 focuses on environmental management and the effects of organizational activities.
